subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS ON TENTH ANNIVERSARY OF ACCESSION TO THRONE
speechtext:
It is my
privilege on behalf of this group at this time to join with the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Laurier in expressing our loyalty to Her Majesty the Queen and in conveying to her on behalf of parliament, in the unanimous sense, our best wishes. For some time, Mr. Speaker, the treasury board has been giving consideration to the question of the language in which government cheques are printed. There has been no uniformity in the practice prevailing heretofore. Cheques have been in use in bilingual 26207-1-37
form in the province of Quebec for some purposes but not for others. Cheques used for the purpose of making payments of any kind in the other nine provinces have been in English only except for some bilingual cheques issued in Ottawa.
The board has decided that the time has come to end the anomaly of this variety of practices and to bring the practice in relation to cheques into harmony with our practice in relation to Canadian currency, money orders and postal remittances, all of which are in bilingual form.
Accordingly, acting in pursuance of the powers conferred on it by parliament in section 33 (1) of the Financial Administration Act, the board has directed that hereafter, as existing stocks of cheque forms and those already on order are depleted, forms printed in both English and French will be adopted in the case of all cheques drawn on the account of the Receiver General.

speechtext:
On Friday the Leader of the Opposition asked what steps are taken

to ensure that goods exported from Canada to Cuba are not originally from the United States, and whether the exporters are asked to give the original source of goods exported to Cuba.
The export control list contains an item which requires an export permit for the reexport from Canada of all goods originating outside Canada. The item is defined in group 9 of the list. The export permit application form requires that the exporter declare the country of origin of the goods, whether any of the goods are wholly or in part of United States origin, and if so what percentage of the total value of the export are goods of United States origin and what percentage of the value of the goods of United States origin are in the same condition as when imported.
Where goods may be exported without an export permit, the exporter is required under the export permit regulations to declare on the customs entry form B-13 that the export does not contain goods imported from the United States that have not been further processed or manufactured in Canada and the export is in accordance with the Export and Import Permits Act and regulations.
The Export and Import Permits Act provides that officers as defined in the Customs Act have, with respect to any goods to which the Export and Import Permits Act applies, all the powers they have under the Customs Act respecting search, detention, seizure, and forfeiture.

On the orders of the day:
Righl Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister): The hon. member for Port Arthur asked me a question yesterday relating to base metal production. He wanted to know what effect, if any, I or the minister responsible can discern in the statement of policy President Kennedy announced last week with regard to stockpiling base metals, and what repercussions it may have here.
The statement by the President of the United States announced the intention to appoint a commission to make a detailed review of United States stockpiling policies, programs and goals in the light of changing defence and strategic requirements and improved technology. The statement indicated his awareness of the intricate and interrelated problems, including the difficulties experienced by certain mineral industries, the impact on world markets and the importance to certain countries in trade in these materials. Then he gave an assurance that no action would be taken which would disrupt commodity prices. Until some indication is available of the findings of that commission, of course no comment could be offered. However, in view of the large stockpile holdings of base metals and other materials important in Canada's export trade, this matter will be kept under close review.
I attach great importance to the assurance given by the President that no action will be taken which will be disruptive to commodity prices.

speechtext: I wish to address a question to the Prime Minister based on a press report that Premier Bennett has suggested a meeting of the premiers to discuss a possible national energy grid. Can the Prime Minister advise the house as to the attitude of the government toward the suggestion?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT OF PENSION
speechtext:
On the matter of the financial implications of this change, I have already indicated to the house that additional outlays are estimated at $113.4 million over the next 12 months. When account is taken of the expected increase in the number of recipients, total federal expenditures under the Old Age Security Act are projected at about $737 million for the coming fiscal year, 1962-63.
This very substantial sum provides striking evidence of the government's concern for the well being of Canada's senior citizens. Nor is our support of senior citizens limited to the old age security program. As hon. members are aware, federal contributions in this regard are also made under the Old Age Assistance Act and the unemployment assistance program. The cost of these two measures is of course shared with the provinces, but the

fact remains that the dominion government carries the bulk of the responsibility for meeting the economic needs of the older people of this country.
By way of illustration I might point out that for the fiscal year 1961-1962 total income maintenance payments under old age security, old age assistance and supplementary allowances are estimated at roughly $708 million. Of this amount the federal government is expected to contribute some $666 million or 94 per cent of the total. The remainder will be provided by the provinces and/or the municipalities.
These figures give an indication of the situation within Canada, but I think it is also interesting to see where we stand on the matter of old age income security as compared with other countries. Let us consider the United States, for example. Unfortunately the latest breakdown of United States outlays is for 1959-1960 so the comparison cannot be as up to date as the one I have cited for Canada alone. Nevertheless I think the comparison is instructive.
In the United States, in 1959-60, payments to aged pensioners under the old age and survivors insurance program together with federal-state outlays for old age assistance amounted to 2.66 per cent of net national income. In Canada, for the same year, total outlays on behalf of senior citizens under old age security, old age assistance and supplementary allowances amounted to 2.41 per cent of net national income. At the same time the Canadian figure is somewhat higher than the relative percentage for another federally organized country, namely Australia. In Australia the corresponding proportion of net national income devoted to old age income security in 1959-60 was 2.30 per cent.
The actions now being taken on old age pensions will of course place Canada in a much more favourable position as measured by the relationship of old age income benefits to net national income. They will also increase the differential previously in our favour with respect to rates of benefit. For example, in June 1960 the average benefit being paid to retired single workers under the United States old age and survivors insurance program was equal to 37.2 per cent of personal income per capita. Here I would stress the work "average" because, as hon. members may be aware, the United States program does not have a flat rate benefit but embodies a graduated system with payments to individuals varying over a wide range. In any event, the average paid in June, 1960 was equivalent to 37.2 per cent of personal income per capita. In Canada, by contrast, the rate being paid to all recipients of old age security stood at 42.9 per cent of personal income per capita.

If we take the case of retired workers with wives eligible for pension, we find that Canada's position is even more favourable. In June, 1960 the average benefit payable in the United States under such circumstances was equal to 66 per cent of average personal income. This was considerably lower than the percentage in Canada for a husband and wife both in receipt of old age security. The benefits paid to all couples in this position in our country worked out to 85.7 per cent of average personal income.
Here I should point out that these comparisons do not take into account subsequent adjustments in the United States program and the proposed increases now being put forward by this government. It is anticipated that when the situation is analysed on the basis of data for 1962, the relevant percentages will place Canada in an even more advantageous position.
I trust that I have not burdened the house too much with statistics, Mr. Speaker, but it seems to me that in this case they are the most effective way of outlining a situation which I am sure is of great interest to all hon. members.
In my opening remarks at the resolution stage preceding introduction of this bill I made reference to the relationship between the changes now being proposed and the contributory pension plan forecast in the speech from the throne. Because of the close connection between these matters I should like to elaborate a little further on our intentions with regard to the contributory program.
As the house is aware, the present government was responsible for having a comprehensive report prepared on this subject by Professor Robert M. Clark. Following exhaustive study of this document and other relevant material, it was decided that a contributory old age, survivors and disability insurance program bearing certain similarities to the United States plan should be established as a logical means of completing the structure of systematic provision for retirement income in Canada. This structure already includes the basic old age security pension, the means test old age assistance pension paid jointly by the provinces and the federal government, the supplementary public assistance payments under the Unemployment Assistance Act paid on a needs test basis by the provinces and the federal government, the many existing industrial pension plans, and finally the registered retirement savings plans that have been a special feature of Canadian experience in recent years.
With the current proposal, one could reasonably claim that the edifice will have been completed without detracting from the existing elements of the structure. In a nutshell,
OZd Age Security Act
our proposal is to complement existing measures through the establishment of a system of old age insurance payments. This is in line with the policy laid down by the Prime Minister on January 13, 1958 as reported on page 3234 of Hansard. At that time the Prime Minister stated as follows:
... the course to be followed would be that it would be in addition to. over and above, old age security.
The benefits under this projected program will be payable to all contributors on reaching retirement age of 65 years or over, and will vary with the size of a person's contributions during his working life. In cases where a contributor dies or becomes disabled before reaching retirement age, his widow and dependant children or he himself if disabled will be able to draw advance benefits from the credits he has built up in this contributory program. If anyone wishes to receive the benefit at an earlier age, an actuarially reduced benefit may be received as early as age 62. As mentioned at the resolution stage yesterday, this provision is available under the old age and survivors insurance program in the United States.
We have no intention of putting heavy additional costs on private industry. Many private pension plans now in operation are making adequate provision for employees enrolled under such plans. To the extent that existing private pension plans are considered to be satisfactory as compared with the; proposed government plan, persons Covered under these plans will be exempt from the compulsory features of the new program.
We do not intend to duplicate private pension coverage for Canadians. Any scheme which loads the costs of a public program on top of existing private schemes will be placing a very heavy burden on the competitive position of Canadian industry. Existing pension plans which provide benefits equal to or better than the proposed government plans should be encouraged to continue their operations. When the United States old age and survivors insurance program commenced in 1937, private pension plans were not widespread in that country. Now, 25 years later, We have in this country many private pension plans which must be recognized in any system of nation-wide old age insurance. Under the recent British legislation it was found advisable to permit existing private pension plans which were considered to be satisfactory to continue operation and to exempt persons covered by them from the graduated supplementary old age pension plan introduced by the British government. This is an aspect of the British program in which we are particularly interested.
A further point I might make is that the new contributory system will be financed by

Old Age Security Act
contributions from employers, employees, and the self-employed who come within its provision.
Yesterday at the resolution stage several hon. members made extremely useful contributions to the debate. However, I am afraid that I cannot say this for the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). I should like to know who actually has been doing the competing for votes. I do not know how anybody could be more inconsistent or more competitive for votes. To me this simply indicates no sense of responsibility whatever. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, this type of thing reminds me of the Liberal promise in 1919 concerning hospital insurance, which finally came to fruition 38 years later. While the actual hospital insurance act was passed when the Liberals were in power, it fell to the Conservatives to implement it.
There is another reference I should like to make. When the hon. member for Essex East was speaking on the resolution yesterday he indicated that the Liberal party was putting forward a plan that was responsible and involved no further taxes, but would be paid

for out of the contributions of individuals. I do not know just what this means. I claim it is only a play on words. Whether the program is provided for from ordinary revenues, from earmarked taxes or from payroll taxes, somebody has to pay for it. These are all levies imposed by parliament. In my view the performance of the hon. member yesterday was simply one of desperation.
Much has been said about the constitutional issue and I am sure more will be said before the debate is finished, but I should like to place on the record again a paragraph which formed part of my speech yesterday. I said then, as found on page 531 of Hansard:
The constitutional question may be raised. When the Liberal government was considering the introduction of unemployment insurance in 1940 the prime minister of the day wrote to the provinces and consulted with them concerning an amendment to the B.N.A. Act. All provinces agreed, and an amendment was obtained stating beyond doubt that the authority for such a program was within federal jurisdiction. Again, in 1951, the Liberal government sought an amendment as a basis for the introduction of the old age security program, and a mutually satisfactory amendment was worked out.
The present government follows the same procedure, Mr. Speaker, and we hear objections. The Liberals say it is not necessary for us to consult the provinces. If the Liberal party is not concerned with provincial rights and due regard for the constitution, that is a matter that I think should be brought before the public now. The program that the government proposes to place before the house involves the provision of benefits to widows, dependant children and disabled persons under a social insurance plan.
The Liberal party issued a pamphlet some weeks ago which claimed to have all the answers, but they have different answers now. I am not too sure whether this clause should be considered part of their platform but at any rate one plank, shall I put it, was the provision of pension benefits to those who are disabled before retirement age, and to widows and orphans. As I understand the situation, that coincides exactly with our plan.
There is no doubt that the advice we have received from the law officers of the crown is simply to the effect that the present section 94A of the B.N.A. Act does not encompass such benefits. Contributory old age pensions as such may be covered, but not benefits for disabled persons and for widows and orphans. I claim that these two gentlemen who spoke yesterday for the Liberal party indicated clearly that they had not read the Clark report. I do not think anything could be clearer from a reading of their speeches.
There will be more speeches today, and I propose to say a few words in reply at the end of the debate. I claim that this is good,

sound, sensible legislation. It is going to be of great benefit to more than 930,000 Canadian citizens, and I should like to commend the bill for early passage by the house.

Mr. Speaker, every time the Minister of National Health and Welfare makes a speech one learns more and more about his amazing technique and his day to day knowledge of the problems that come under his administration. He gave us more details today about a plan that is not yet in existence, but which the government seems now, at long last, at least to have in the back of its mind as something that some day it might do if perchance it ever has the opportunity again.
The minister certainly reflected the dilemma in which members of the government find themselves when they come to examine the record of the various Liberal governments in the field of social welfare. They have to go back to 1919 to try to find whether promises made by a Liberal administration have been fulfilled. Of course this is not a new disc. One hears it in the house from time to time, emanating from ministerial benches, but it is significant that they never complain about failure of Liberal governments under Mackenzie King or under Mr. St. Laurent to implement promises made in the area of social legislation.
There is no complaint by hon. members opposite that the Liberal party failed to carry out the assurances given by Mr. Mackenzie King in 1925 as to his intentions regarding old age pensions. Hon. gentlemen do not complain, nor do they find any justification for saying that Liberal governments failed to implement promises in the field of family allowances or with regard to old age assistance or blindness allowances. They could not under any circumstances, of course, make any charge about non-fulfilment of promises with regard to disability pensions because no such promise was made by a Liberal government. It was after Mr. St. Laurent's return to office the second time that he caused the Disabled Persons Act to be introduced in the house, which has provided assistance to so many people in this country and in connection with which we are to be happily confronted with an amendment some time later during the course of our proceedings.
Nor do we hear any complaint from the government side that the Liberals have brought forward legislation to assist the provinces in carrying out their constitutional obligations in the field of health care. It will be remembered that in 1945 the federal government put before the provinces what has been termed a package deal. This was
26207-1-38i
Old Age Security Act
a program covering health and welfare, a comprehensive program most of which has since been realized. There was no obligation on the part of the government of Canada in relation to any promise that it had made to make grants in aid to the provinces, to assist them in laying the foundation for a health insurance system in this country.
One could cover the whole area of health and welfare activity and one would not find that hon. members opposite have ever complained about the lack of the Liberal government in the fulfilment of its promises. I believe, sir, that is a record of which we may well be proud in this party. We take the view that promises made to the Canadian people during an election, or during the course of the fulfilment of an official obligation on the part of various ministers and of the government as a whole, are solemn promises that must be respected by those who make them. We do not take the view once expressed by the Minister of National Revenue in this house that there was a difference between a commitment made by a government to parliament and a commitment made by government to the people of Canada during the course of an election. The latter kind of promise the Minister of National Revenue, in his characteristically able manner, suggested was a promise that no government had to keep. This is not the view of the Liberal party. What I have said about our fulfilment of promises in the field of health and welfare supports what I have said about our respect for our commitments to parliament and to the people of Canada.
I wish I could say the same thing for this government. We have had an example today, through the admission of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, that his government has not fulfilled a solemn promise made to the Canadian people. Perhaps last night the Minister of Labour let the cat out of the bag. After I had recited some of the essential features of the plan which the Leader of the Opposition had enunciated on January 5, the Minister of Labour indicated clearly what was in his mind, what was in the mind of the Prime Minister and his colleagues, with regard to the pledges which they put forward in this field to the Canadian people. The Minister of Labour exclaimed "Election promises. ' This is exactly what the government is thinking, that is the context in which they place their views of social welfare in this country; election promises.
The most outstanding election promise made by this government in the field of social welfare was with regard to a program that has so obviously agitated the Minister of National Health and Welfare and has caused

Old Age Security Act
wide wonderment. Yesterday when he was introducing a simple amendment which we support, as we do this bill, involving an inadequate increase in the universal old age security plan he went on, not to talk about that increase, but rather to indicate that it did not have the same significance as the contributory plan. He went on to talk about that plan, not the plan of the government but the plan the Liberal party put forward on January 5.
He gave us some details of that plan. He also gave us some criticisms of the plan put forward by the Liberal party which would establish a national minimum pension of $75 a month, not $65 as is proposed by this bill. This plan would be based upon contributions by the Canadian people which would result in much larger pensions, which would be paid for by contributions by Canadian citizens. Then today we had an amazing tour de force on the part of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He came back again to our plan. He did not discuss the bill. I do riot believe the minister said five sentences about the bill that is immediately before the house. What did he do? He talked about the Liberal contributory plan, the plan that is going to give the Canadian people a national minimum pension of $75. That is the plan about which he talked today. He talked about it at greater length even than he did yesterday, and Clearly established in the minds of all of us the apprehension and agitation that has taken hold of those who sit on the ministerial benches.
They' do not like this plan because they know that, plaCed alongside what the government is now proposing, this plan put forward by the Liberal leader will commend itself to the Canadian people as a more comprehensive way of dealing with the problem of old age security in this Country. Not only did he discuss our plan' in greater detail, but he discussed in greater detail the kind of plan which was envisaged by1 the Prime Minister in November, 1957, as well as in the months of January and February, 1958, when he made the solemn Commitment to the Canadian people that his government would forthwith introduce a national contributory scheme modelled on the lines of the social security system in the United States.
He talked about that today in greater detail than he did yesterday. Why did he do this? Why did he not tell the provinces, why did the Prime Minister not tell the provinces, some of the details of that plan when he wrote to them in the month of January asking for concurrence in the constitutional amendment to enable the government to introduce a, contributory scheme? Why did the Prime Minister not tell the provinces the details

which we were given today in greater precision? I suggest that the reason is obvious. The government has no detailed plan. The only plan the government has evolved since is one that was evolved under pressure, because of the exposition of the Liberal plan to provide for a national minimum pension, as enunciated by the Liberal leader on January 5.
Today the Minister of National Health and Welfare has given us more details than he did yesterday only because, after reading the morning newspapers, after listening to television and radio, he found his own plan had been engulfed and overwhelmed by public interest in the Liberal plan. Then he found it necessary, and I suspect at the bidding of the Prime Minister, to talk more glowingly, more eloquently, more vigorously about something that may come some time in the uncertain future. This is the situation in the face of the fact that this government has caused to be prepared the report on economic security for the aged in the United States and Canada by Dr. Robert M. Clark, which was presented to parliament in. two volumes in 1959.
We all know the circumstances under which that report was made. These circumstances were outlined last night. If I may remind hon. gentlemen, we were told that the Prime Minister had indicated to the Canadian people and to parliament that he was anxious in 1958 to adopt a system similar to the social security plan in the United States; that there was going to be a careful study. Notwithstanding the attitude taken by the Minister of Finance, notwithstanding the attitude taken by the Prime Minister in 1958, notwithstanding the advice officials in the Department of National Health and Welfare may have offered, the government was going to make a study and that study would be followed by action by this government. The unfulfilled promise in the field of social welfare for which this government must stand indicted, is that of causing the Canadian people to believe it was going to bring forward a plan based on the Clark report. Now all we get from this government and this active Minister of National Health and Welfare, just on the eve of an election, is a portrayal of some vague conception the government might have with regard to something that it might do in the uncertain future regarding the adoption in Canada of the old age security and survivor system implemented in the United States.
Well, Mr. Speaker, promises made to the Canadian people are not to be respected. The Minister of National Revenue said there is a difference between a promise made to parliament and a promise made to the Canadian people, and the Minister of Labour said

"an election promise". Is this vague recital of a plan, whose soul will take on form in the long distant future, to be regarded simply as a promise? I say that the Minister of National Health and Welfare holds a responsible position under the crown, a position which in this country has attached to it the respect and authority which parliament has conferred upon it.
This government has treated the aged people of our country in an irresponsible manner, such as has rarely been exhibited in the parliament of Canada, and no one has done that more than the right hon. Prime Minister. Today, on the second day of this debate, he tabled letters which he should have tabled yesterday. If the consent of all the premiers had not been received, certainly consent from at least the majority of them had come in, and we should have been afforded the opportunity of examining those letters for the purposes of our discussion yesterday, letters which were reluctantly tabled by the Prime Minister.
Today we find some of the premiers taking the position that they would like to examine the proposal put forward by the Prime Minister of Canada with regard to a proposed amendment that might lead to the establishment in this country of a system somewhat similar to the social security plan in the United States. Here is what the premier of Quebec said, among other things, in his letter to the Prime Minister of Canada on January 24:
(Translation):
I sincerely believe it to be essential that your government supply the provinces with the details of your plan before asking them to propose to their legislatures that they agree to a constitutional amendment.
(Text):
What is the premier asking? He is saying "before giving our consent we would like to know what it is you want to do; we would like to have some idea of the plan you have in mind; we would like to have some precision as to the kind of amendment you seek." It well may be that the premier of Quebec and other premiers would take the position that the amendment obtained in 1950 to the British North America Act, section 94A, was wide enough to permit the federal government to embark upon a contributory plan, even along the lines so vaguely conceived and projected today by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Why were the provinces not given at least the details which the minister gave yesterday? Certainly there could be no justification for not giving the further details he gave today with regard to what the government had in mind
5*5
Old Age Security Act concerning the adoption of a system similar to that in the United States, the United Kingdom and the Scandinavian countries.
The reason is that in spite of the Clark report, in spite of the promises of the Prime Minister, in spite of the lapse of four years, he has waited until this time to give precision to something which he said he had in his mind and heart in November, 1957, and upon which he later elaborated on January 18, 1958. Let the Minister of National Health and Welfare not talk about promises. Let him not belittle the plan that was enunciated by the Liberal leader on January 5; because that plan, based upon careful consideration and study and supported by the evidence and documentation in the Clark report, is a responsible scheme which the Canadian people are demanding, and for which they supported the Prime Minister when, during the election of 1958, he told them he was going to supplement the existing universal system with a system similar to that in the United States.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare, in bringing forward his proposal today for an increase under the Old Age Security Act, neglected to say something which he neglects to observe on all occasions, that once again he was bringing in an amendment to an act introduced by a Liberal administration. He neglected to say that the Old Age Security Act is the only act of its kind to be found in any country in the world, that it is the only act which provides for the elimination of a means test. It is the only old age security act which extends benefit to all Canadian citizens when they reach the qualifying age of 70 years.
The minister spoke as though the Old Age Security Act, bringing benefit to the limited extent it does to over 900,000 people, was a product of the present administration. Does the minister deny the reports in the Globe and Mail and elsewhere to that effect? It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that this process of educating, in which I am currently engaged, has come not too soon if I correctly understood the implications of the question asked by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm.
The scheme outlined by the Leader of the Opposition will make it possible for all Canadians to take part in a contributory pension plan geared to the growth in our economy. It will not require any addition to taxes because the plan calls for a payment of benefits out of contributions that will grow during the first ten years, enabling the giving of pensions in larger amounts, proportionate to the earnings of the contributor. Added to the existing federal old age pension this plan will establish a new national minimum of $75 a month for a retired person at age 70 and $140 for a married couple. Even the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm will some day, when he grows older, qualify under this plan introduced by the Liberal party.
The minimum for retired people aged 70 or over makes provision for those who have not had the opportunity to contribute under the Liberal plan. The size of pensions will rise year by year, as people retire after contributing to the new plan. Full pension rates-a good proportion of most people's earnings- will be reached in ten years. These pensions will be available from age 65.
We can speak with some authority in this matter because it was Liberal governments that introduced the universal old age pension and, in co-operation with the provinces, made old age assistance available to people between 65 and 70 who are in need.
Our plan is a supplement to private saving. The minister spoke of private saving and private pension plans. While many companies now have good pension schemes, the majority of the working population is not covered by them. There are other problems as well. While younger people can build up good pensions by the time they retire, new private plans cannot enable older workers to do so at contribution rates they can afford. Also, workers
Old Age Security Act
who lose or change their jobs are liable to lose pension rights. This is a serious obstacle to people moving between jobs and is therefore bad for economic efficiency as well as for the individual. Such problems, in the context of our modern industrial society, must be met and dealt with. As people live longer, the assurance of an adequate income during retirement becomes more and more important to us all.
I want the Minister of National Health and Welfare to follow these details and to contrast them with the very nebulous and uncoordinated plan which he so vaguely enunciated today, perhaps because it is vague. I want him to consider why it was not possible, when he had access to the same information in the Clark report to which we had access, to bring forward at this time, if not in 1959 when it should have been brought forward, a contributory scheme based on that in the United States and so strongly advocated by the Prime Minister.
When our plan is in full operation the pension each person gets will be related to what he has contributed. That is why I said it does not involve any rise in taxes. As in most private plans, contributions will be made by wage and salary earners and also by employers on their behalf. When a man changes his job his full pension rights will move with him. Contributions will be a small percentage of earnings. People who are self-employed may join the plan, which will be well worth while for most of them. Everyone will be able to choose between taking the pension at age 65 or waiting and taking a larger pension at age 70.
Today the minister spoke about this projected plan of his as one providing an opportunity for people to begin to take pensions at age 62. That is the provision in the United States. He did not explain how that would be done, nor did he mention what I pointed out last night, namely that our old age assistance scheme provides for old age assistance pensions to widows and unmarried women at age 60. No comment was made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare on this feature. He seemed to be overly obsessed with our contributory scheme and to have overlooked some of the other incidental results.
There is another feature of our plan that the minister has failed to note. He will be bringing in shortly a resolution to provide for an increase in the basic amount of disability pensions. He said nothing about what this scheme of ours will do in regard to disability pensions. He of course said nothing about the fact that it was a Liberal government under

In view of your observations, Mr. Speaker, I agree that technically that may be the case. But since our contributory plan was discussed and since the minister overlooked mentioning one important feature of it, I thought I was within my rights, as I strongly believe I am. However, I will not continue, as I think the important point has been made and I hope it will be observed by the minister.
Both contributions and pension benefits will apply only up to a moderate level of earnings. The Liberal plan will not operate to benefit rich people who do not need government action. It will not discourage private pension plans or other saving for retirement by those who can afford more. There will be good reason for continued saving in all forms. Among people with moderate incomes there will be a particular incentive to organize private pension plans for earlier retirement.
Then we go on in this plan to provide, as I indicated earlier, assistance to those between the ages of 65 and 69. Those are the features

of this plan which the minister in his criticism has failed to underline. He failed clearly to establish that we were providing a national pension plan to which the individual would contribute according to his earnings. He failed to point out that from the fund that would be created there would be paid a minimum supplementary pension of $20 a month at age 70, making the total federal pension $75 a month for a single person and $140 for a married couple. He failed to point out that, in co-operation with the provinces, this plan indicated we were ready to increase old age assistance not to $65, as is proposed by the government, but to $75 a month, and that we were prepared to make old age assistance available to unmarried women and widows at age 60; and that we were prepared to pay supplementary old age assistance of $20 a month to a married woman at age 70 and over in cases where the $140 a month pension available to a married couple left them in need of further assistance.
He failed to point out that under our scheme which he criticized it was proposed to pay to those retiring after contributing to the fund, pensions which would rise during a 10-year transition period until they equalled a good proportion of the earnings of each man or woman while working. He did not say that the individual would be enabled to choose between a pension at age 65 or a larger pension at 70. He failed to point out that we would provide pension benefits to those who were disabled and to widows and to orphans.
I withdraw that statement. He did mention that our scheme dealt with widows, survivors and dependants, but he sought to establish that, because of that fact, the present section 94A of the British North America Act created a situation which meant that this parliament was not competent to provide for such a scheme.
With regard to that problem I can only repeat what I said yesterday and now say in the presence of the Minister of Justice. I can very well understand that there might be some difference of opinion and judgment as to whether all parts of this contributory scheme put forward by the Liberal party are in compliance with our constitutional provisions. I can only say, as I established yesterday, that responsible legal opinion in this country, the opinion of those we have consulted, is that there can be no question of the constitutionality of the simple pension on a contributory basis following the United States pattern; and that under the aspect theory there can be no doubt about the constitutionality of pensions to survivors or to dependants. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), who may or may not speak on this matter,

knows, of course, the cases of Hodge v. the Queen, Tennant v. the Union Bank, Grand Trunk Railway v. Canada, Proprietory Articles Trade Association v. Attorney General for Canada and others, all of which deal with the aspect theory and which hold that subjects which in one aspect or for one purpose may fall within section 92 may in another aspect or for another purpose fall within section 91 of the British North America Act.
But having said this I admit that there may be room for a difference of opinion. If it is argued by the law officers of the crown that this scheme is outside our competence I am sure the government cannot take the position that to provide a pension for an individual is unconstitutional. I have before me the letter of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) addressed to the provinces on the 17th of January, and in the fourth paragraph the Prime Minister says:
The law officers of the crown advise me that this authority would permit parliament to enact a contributory, graduated old age pension plan but would not permit the inclusion of benefits payable under certain circumstances to widows and children, nor to contributors who become disabled before they are old.
The Prime Minister says there clearly and unmistakably that at least one aspect of this project is constitutional. It is, he says, within our constitutional competence "to enact a contributory, graduated old age pension plan", apart altogether from the benefits to survivors, dependants and disabled people.
I simply ask the Prime Minister this question on the basis of this statement in his letter. If it is clear that there is no doubt about the constitutionality in this one particular, what excuse can the government offer now for not having proceeded at least with regard to that aspect of the problem under section 94A of the British North America Act. If there is a valid reason for not proceeding with regard to that one particular then I say to the government, what excuse can it possibly offer for telling us only in the month of February, 1962, that there is this constitutional impediment? Why could we not have been told that last September? Why were we not told it last July when we were discussing pensions under estimates of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and when I outlined the kind of scheme envisaged by the Liberal party at the national Liberal convention in 1958? Why were we not told in 1959? Why were we not told in 1958 by the Prime Minister who said, "We are going to have a study made of this whole business and then we are going to enact legislation in this parliament based on the social security system in the United States"?
Old Age Security Act
The government will not be able to hide behind this constitutional impediment, if such exists. It has had all the time in the world to consult with the provinces, all the time in the world to bring forward an amendment. The only reason I can possibly see why they have not taken this step is that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) is still in charge of the government and is still the boss. He is not the prime minister but because of his well known views about contributory pensions he was able to cause the government to postpone month after month, year after year, something that the Prime Minister said in 1958 we were going to get at the earliest possible moment once his government came into being.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) is here today. I ask him to consider whether a plan involving contributions by employers, employees and self-employed to a national fund for the purpose of providing a simple pension is not within our constitutional rights, whether such a plan providing for the payment of benefits at 65 or 70, ultimately scaled to contributions, is not within our constitutional rights. I ask him to tell us what constitutional difficulty arises out of a provision for an interim increase and adjustment of existing old age pensions and, in co-operation with the provinces, the provision of plans for old age assistance. What constitutional difficulty is there with regard to the payment of benefits to persons permanently disabled and prevented from working until retirement age? If there is one, why were we not told that three years ago?
So I say, Mr. Speaker, with full confidence in what I am saying, that we in the Liberal party in bringing forward this plan have taken a responsible step, a step that will not only provide more than $65 a month as envisaged by this bill, which we support, but will provide a national minimum of $75 and will provide increasing amounts to Canadian citizens in the years to come after the fund has gone through a period of maturity.
I live in the city of Windsor, on the Canada-United States border. The Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Halpenny) from London lives not far away. Those of us in that area are familiar with the United States plan. We see individuals living in Windsor who have worked in Detroit and are drawing pensions as high as $300 a month. This is the kind of plan which the Liberal party is proposing, a plan that does not add one cent to the obligations of the government of Canada or to the Canadian taxpayer as such, a plan that is paid for out of contributions by the

Old Age Security Act
beneficiaries of the plan. Some may say, why did you not bring that plan forward when you were in office?

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-6 to amend the Interest Act (finance charges).
He said: The purpose of this bill is to provide some protection for the purchaser of credit against the practice which has become so widespread, namely the neglect to outline the cost of servicing that credit, and the cost of carrying it, in respect to the normal accepted procedure in so far as interest is concerned. Should this bill be accepted by the house, and become law, it would provide a penalty for failure to outline total charges, and their percentage relation to the principal involved. In addition to that penalty, failure to act in accordance with the bill would cancel the rights of the lender to any interest charges on such a contract.
Some hon. members may say that these are drastic penalties, but I maintain they are needed if the present situation is to be corrected. Business practice in Canada has accepted the practice of displaying price tags. Indeed, that is one of the foundations of competitive trade. Our society has accepted the
Interest Act
principle that the customer is entitled to know the price of his purchase. The practice has been zealously guarded by our governments, particularly, in regard to financial transactions. Both the Bank Act and Interest Act set out the limits within which interest may be charged. Promissory notes carry the rate of interest on their face, prominently displayed. Certain types of bonds are required to show in express terms the interest they will yield. The reason for this practice has been that these requirements prevent misunderstandings which might place upon one or other of the parties to such a transaction a burden or obligation of which he was not fully aware. Our banking institutions have discharged their responsibilities, generally, within the confines of the Bank Act. The general rule followed by these institutions can be best described as loans for productive purposes. That left a considerable void in modern society's financial requirements. The desire of enterprising merchandisers and manufacturers to maintain volume in their production pattern has necessitated a form of credit to finance these transactions. In some cases at least the money required for this financing has been secured from banks at an agreed rate and is provided at varying rates to customers who desire to purchase goods on credit. Payroll cities have become dependant upon this type of financing. Indeed, there are many cases which could be used to illustrate the mutual advantages this system of merchandising provides for the customer and the merchant as well. Because of the monthly payroll characteristic of incomes in these cities, the practice has developed of pricing goods at so much down and so much a month for so many months, without any clear indication of the percentage costs of carrying this service. Some of the finance companies have been equally reluctant to reveal these pertinent facts in their transactions. This situation has obscured the true cost of such credit, and it is my contention the risks involved are most minute when a loan is based on knowledge of the customers security of income. This factor is to my mind one of the major reasons for the practice which has developed, quite apart from the pure encouragement that monthly payments have for merchandising purposes alone. The extent to which finance purchasing has become prevalent is the best denial of the assertion that there are great risks involved. The desire for obscurity in their transactions is motivated by the desire to continue to enjoy the present rate of return on these transactions.
The question that we must ask ourselves is, first: is the customer or purchaser of credit entitled to know in clear simple terms the

Interest Act
cost of the service he is securing? Second, is it physically possible for the merchandizer or financier to provide this information without undue effort? I believe both these questions can be answered in the affirmative. There are some people who believe that a bill of this nature should exclude any reference to mortgage loans and the like. I should like to cite an example of what has taken place in some instances in Canada during the last few years. I refer hon. members to the "Ontario Reports" and the "Ontario Weekly Notes" of June 16, 1961 pertaining to the York county court, and I should like to read part of a case described as Scott and Manor Investments Limited. It reads as follows:
Scott and his wife were the owners in February, 1958 of 75 Roebuck Drive, Scarborough. This house had been purchased by them in 1955 for $13,500 and at the time of the borrowing transaction in question there was owing upon the house about $10,000 by way of a first N.H.A. mortgage and between $500 and $600 on a second mortgage on the property.
At the time of the transaction this small second mortgage was falling due and there was a balance due in respect to the purchase of a motorcar. Scott in his affidavit asserts that he was attracted to Manor Investments by an advertisement of theirs in the public press to the effect that mortgages could be arranged without bonus. Pursuant thereto Scott attended at the office of Manor Investments and there he signed a number of documents; a mortgage agreement dated 11th February 1958, which seems to set out particulars of the application to the company for a loan which required payments of $45 monthly, for both principal and interest at 61 per cent per annum. This is signed by Scott, and in paragraph 1 it provides to pay the company an arranging commission of $125.
There is another document 20th February 1958 called collateral advantage bonus agreement. This provides for a mortgage loan of $3,200, and interest is stated to be at 12 per cent repayable $45 including principal and interest; and it states:
We W. J. Scott and H. Scott further agree that we will accept the sum of $2,500 as the net proceeds due under the said mortgage; the balance of $700 being a bonus to Manor Investments.
Then there is a mortgage dated 20th February 1958, which is for $3,200 which bears interest at 12 per cent with monthly payments of $45 including both principal and interest and which states that the interest shall be computed half yearly not in advance, on the 17th days of August and February in each year after the date of the mortgage. The mortgage was for three years to fall due 17th February 1961.
Now this mortgage was signed by the Scotts and they received by way of the proceeds of this transaction, less legal fees and disbursements and an inspection fee, the sum of $2,375 which money was used to pay off the current indebtedness of the borrowers on the car and on the existing second mortgage as above stated. At that time a statement was issued dated the 27th February, 1958, by Manor Investments showing the amount of the loan $3,200, the bonus stated to be "Cost-precalculated risk $700", and "arranging commission $125", and then the other items of disbursements,
In this case the borrower actually received only $2,375. When we come to assess the interest on this loan we find the borrowers were charged a bonus of $700, an arranging fee of

$125 and interest on $3,200 over a three-year period at 12 per cent, which amounted to $1,152 or a total, in all, of $1,977. This amounts to an interest of $659 per year on an average, which works out to something over 27.5 per cent. The magistrate charged with deciding this case said it would be somewhat less in the following two years.
I do not think I need to read any further in this connection. This is just one case which indicates what can take place as things are today. There are further cases mentioned in the reports I have here but I do not wish to take up the time of the committee by reading more than I have in this regard.
Before resuming my seat I shall read the contents of the bill so it will appear in the record for those who wish to examine it. It offers an amendment to the Interest Act by adding section 16, amending sections 17 and 18. The bill reads as follows:
1. The Interest Act is amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 15 thereof, the following section: "Finance Charges".
16.	In sections 17 and 18,
(a)	"credit debt" is the debt that is the consideration in whole or in part under any executory contract whatsoever for an interest in real or personal property, or for a service, or for both interest and service; and
(b)	"finance charge" means any and every debt whatsoever stipulated for or exacted on any credit debt and includes, but without restricting the generality of the foregoing, interest, brokerage fees and charges, bonus, service charge, subscription, dues, discount, commission, or premium.
17.	Every person who carries on the business of extending credit, either directly or as a service in the course of another business, and in the course of that business extends credit, on which finance charges are stipulated for or exacted, to another person is guilty of an offence unless, before credit is so extended, he furnishes that other person an express written statement of
(a)	the total amount of the finance charges to be chargeable to that other person on the credit so extended; and
(b)	the ' amount of the credit and the rate of percentage which the finance charges bear to that amount, computed annually and not in advance.
Perhaps this is a good opportunity to say that the purpose of this bill is to make a credit financier criminally liable when he does not, before the credit transaction, clearly disclose in writing to the debtor the cost of the. credit calculated as a total dollar amount and as a yearly percentage of the credit amount to be granted. This criminal liability attaches only to the individual or company granting the credit in the original instance and in the course of a business or as ancillary to the operation of another business.
The liability does not attach to the person who grants credit, but not as a business; nor does the liability attach to the person

who takes over the credit transaction, after it legally exists and is operating, from the original creditor.
However, failure by the original creditor to make full disclosure results also in a civil penalty to the original creditor in that the finance charges, including interest, are null and void and uncollectable by way of contract debt, damages under a bond, seizure and sale, repossession or any other right and remedy.
As a consequence, an assignment of the original creditor's rights and remedies only assigns a nullity in so far as the finance charges are concerned. The finance charges only survive for the benefit of the debtor who has paid them, in whole or in part; in such case, he may recover them by legal action or by set-off against any unpaid principal.
There may be those who will say this bill is unconstitutional. I would refer them to section 91 of the British North America Act and to subsections 18 dealing with bills of exchange and promissory notes, 19 dealing with interest and 27 dealing with the jurisdiction in criminal law. I believe it is clearly established under this provision that a bill of this nature may emanate from the federal jurisdiction.
I shall say nothing more and in taking my seat I commend to hon. members of the house the bill I have introduced. I believe the principle of this measure is a good one and I remind the house that it is the principle of the bill that is at stake at this time.

I regret that this house does not more frequently take the opportunity of having a vote on second reading of public bills. I think it is good to have votes and indicate our position. The sponsor of this bill, I am sure, would be the first to agree that if the measure passed second reading today it would still be a long way from being the law of the land. Many things could happen. For instance, it could be defeated in committee. It could be defeated on third reading. It could be caught in the dissolution at the end of this week or at some other stage. It might get rejection in the other place. Hence if it passes today, this would merely be the first hurdle. However, it would be an important hurdle, Mr. Speaker, and it would demonstrate to the country that at least a majority of the members of parliament feel it is time that firms in the business of making loans or providing instalment credit did the thing which I suggest is fair, aboveboard and frank, namely inform the

Interest Act
person who is obtaining this credit of the total finance charges and of the interest rate involved.
This measure has nothing to do with the kind of measure that I have been advocating so often with regard to the setting of a ceiling. If a ceiling were set and if the law were enforced, protection like this would not be as necessary. It might be desirable but it certainly would not be as necessary. All this measure does is to say that if a business firm is providing a service by way of loan or by way of instalment credit it should do the fair and straightforward thing, should tell the customer the interest charge being levied and should set it out in writing in the contract.
I think this is the kind of proposal that would get the support of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) who is a distinguished member of this house and has had a long experience in the business field. While I know that he has disagreed with me in times gone by over some of the harsh things I have said about certain business firms in the credit field, I believe he will support the suggestion contained in this measure, namely that companies shall set out the interest and carrying charges that are being levied.
We have this particular measure, the measure before the other place, and Bill No. C-23 in my name having to do with advertising by small loans companies which, if passed and if it became law, would require that in any advertising that is done the interest be set out. In these measures we are dealing with this general problem. I must say that these propositions have received a great deal of attention across this country from time to time and in my judgment have a very substantial measure of support amongst the public and amongst ordinary financial institutions, and very frequently have the support of credit unions and the credit union central organization. The credit union is doing a worth-while service at what is usually a very low interest rate. I feel that it is only proper and fair that all companies, including credit unions, should set forth the interest rates that are being charged in any of the transactions that may be made. Under the circumstances prevailing, having regard to the history of support for this measure and for other similar measures we have had in the past, I believe that this afternoon this measure can be dealt with on a non-political and nonpartisan basis and that it is the kind of measure that should command general support from all parties in this house. Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on Bill No. C-6, to amend the Interest Act, I should like to say at the outset that I am much in favour of what is spelled out in this amendment. As I understand the purpose of the bill, it is to make a credit financier criminally liable when he does not, before the credit transaction, clearly disclose in writing to the debtor the cost of the credit calculated as a total dollar amount and as a yearly percentage of the credit amount to be granted.
It is my understanding that if the bill comes into force it will mean that any company that sells to a person on credit or time payments must disclose what the interest charges will be when the note comes due. I must congratulate the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Nasserden) on bringing in this bill, and I am sure it will meet with the approval of many people who have had anything to do with credit financiers or the purchasing of goods on time payments.
This does not mean that many credit financiers are not sincere in the transactions in which they are involved. The bill will actually apply to the unscrupulous credit financiers who may take advantage of a person who is not very familiar with financial transactions and is surprised in the end at the rate of interest when he has to pay his bill.
I must say that times have changed from what they were many years ago. There are many people in our country today who are on salaries and are paid only once a month. They have to go to a credit financier because they wish to buy something for which they are not able to pay cash at the time. As a result they must sign a note and many of them are not familiar with interest charges. That is why I am very much in favour of this bill to amend the act. Those people who sign credit notes will then be in a position to know what they have to pay when they buy something on time payments or what they will have to pay if by reason of unforeseeable circumstances they cannot make the payments as set out in the note.
I am sure that many people have been wanting such an amendment for years. Since I came to the House of Commons, bills or motions to this effect have been introduced from time to time in which it has been provided that credit financiers must disclose

Mr. Speaker, the bill before us this afternoon places before hon. members a very worthy principle, but I must point out that there are certain aspects of it with regard to which it would not be practical so far as its application is concerned. Let me be clear, Mr. Speaker, that in so far as this measure relates to the disclosure of cost and the rate of interest charged, I have no quarrel with it. There is one aspect of this bill which I do not think is practical, and I intend to indicate how this matter was dealt with in a more practical manner in the statutes of Ontario.
First of all, we want to make this a workable instrument; we do not want to defeat the purpose of the bill. There are a number of problems which have not yet been settled. The first one is just how far we can extend the meaning of interest to bring it within the jurisdiction of the federal government. It is quite true that under the constitution the federal government has exclusive jurisdiction to deal with interest. However, when you start adding certain charges to the definition of interest, then you introduce a question as to whether or not those charges fall within the property and civil rights provision. This question was raised in the other place during the introduction of a measure by Senator Croll. I do not believe the question has been resolved.
Another difficulty is the inclusion of all persons in the wording of a section, so that the bill does not become discriminatory. If this measure is to be applied fairly it must cover all persons and not just those who are normally in the business of lending money. If you read the definition as it is here, it does include those who are directly involved in the business of lending money or indirectly involved in lending money in connection with another business. However, the definition does not include those persons who have acquired a certain amount of wealth and who enter the mortgage field, quite apart

from their regular business. Those persons dealing in second mortgages should be included because that is a field about which there has been a great deal of complaint.
This problem, as it relates to mortgages in the province of Ontario, was dealt with in chapter 67 of the statutes of 1960, when the mortgage brokers registration act was passed. This act provides that people dealing in mortgages should be registered and should comply with the terms of the act. Under regulation 46, made under this act which deals with the disclosure of information, we find that this type of information is required, as set out in section 4:
Subsection 1
Every registered broker shall keep and maintain a record showing,
(a)	The repayment terms of each mortgage;
(b)	The total amount actually paid or to be paid to the mortgagor on each mortgage;
(c)	The fees, expenses, costs and other charges required to be borne by the mortgagor in respect of each mortgage transaction;
(d)	The particulars of any related agreement.
Subsection 2 reads:
Every registered broker shall deliver to the mortgagor the information required by subsection 1 on a form approved by the superintendent and shall obtain proof of delivery.
Now, if this can be done in respect of mortgages it can be done in respect to other types of loans and credits. My big quarrel with the present measure is with section 17 (b) which reads:
(b) the amount of the credit and the rate or percentage which the finance charges bear to that amount, computed annually and not in advance.
My complaint is that this is a rather vague provision. The way in which interest might be computed is rather difficult. If a mortgage is discounted the interest might be set out at 6 per cent, but it will actually be more. I feel that when you are creating a criminal offence and putting the responsibility on a person to set out the correct information, you must make the terms of the measure simple so that all people can understand them. If you do not do that, people might be convicted of a criminal offence when, in fact, they would not be sure how the charges should be com-1-puted in accordance with the act. I do not believe it is necessary for a person to know the percentage which the finance charges bear to the loan. This is not the important thing. The important thing for him to know is how much he has to pay in dollars and cents for this loan or the mortgage which he may receive.	: j)
One practical difficulty which may be encountered in connection with mortgages may be where the mortgage term is five years and

it is amortized over a period of 15 years. Tiiese charges would have to be based on the five-year period because the mortgage is said to be for a five-year period. The mortgage rhight contain the privilege of renewal and if it were renewed for a period of 10 years, then the interest calculated on the 10-year period would be different from the interest calculated on the five-year period. These are some of the practical difficulties which might be experienced in the application of this bill.
As X say, I believe this is a principle which should be studied and applied, perhaps in the same manner as it has been applied in Ontario in respect of mortgages. No matter how we might spell these things out, how we might deal with these situations, there are always those who will try to get around the law. I have in my hands some papers relating to a situation in which the Citizens Finance Company made a loan to an elderly couple. The terms were clearly set out. There was an added feature in that if they paid a premium the loan would be insured so that if the husband passed away the loan would be paid. On the basis of this provision, they paid their premium quite satisfied that they had a good loan. Unfortunately, a month ago the husband died. Now the company claims a mistake was made and the insurance policy should not have been issued because the man was too old at the time. They accepted the premiums, however. Now they are trying to entice the widow to go in and accept a receipt for the amount of the premium and release the company. Of course, having done that she would then be responsible for the loan.
This is the type of thing we have to eradicate and make sure that the finance companies who operate in this country adhere to a higher standard of ethics. This bill, Mr. Speaker, and other bills that have come before this house continually in relation to this subject point out the need for revamping the Interest Act, the Small Loans Act, and so on, but only after a careful study. I would suggest that the proper manner in which this study could be carried out would be under order in council PwC. 1961-1484, under which the royal commission was set up to study the financial system in Canada, which includes the banks and other institutions. Under its terms the commissioners by virtue of part I of the Inquiries Act may enquire into and report upon the structure and methods of operation of the Canadian finance system, including the banking and monetary system, and the institutions apd processes involved in the flow of funds through the capital market. Section B(2) of
Interest Act
the] order in council says the commission may inquire into the Bank of Canada Act,, the Quebec Savings Bank Act-;and other relevant federal legislation.	.
I would be happier had the terms of reference been broadened to spell out and include study of the Interest Act and the Small Loans Act. However, I think the terms are broad enough and I hope the commission, which is to be headed by Chief Justice Porter, will take under advisement and study all these acts to ensure that we do have a co-ordinated interest act and co-ordinated regulations affecting small loan companies throughout the country. There are so many instances of divided jurisdiction that unless we have coordination between the federal and provincial authorities we shall not have effective control.
In closing I strongly urge that this whole matter, which has been brought before the house so many times, be brought to the attention of the commissioners for their care and study.

First, in talking on this bill and on bills such as the Interest Act and Small Loans Act, the practice has arisen of illustrating points by reference to particularly bad cases of harsh treatment by finance companies and other institutions. There are instances where people borrow money when they should not, particularly where they have not properly investigated their chances of repaying it, where they have not had the benefit of advice on the business they are entering into as to its earning capacity, and where they have not properly understood the value of money and the necessity of repaying it. In this country there are many finance companies who honestly and earnestly sit down with prospective borrowers and try very hard to make sure they know what they are doing and know whether they have the capacity to repay on the terms they are borrowing. They want to make sure a borrower understands the terms on which he is borrowing because they understand that squeezing repayments out of a man is the worst kind of advertising for their business. I shall admit this is only part of the story but I think we are sometimes remiss in dealing with such matters. What we ought to do is protect these people from essentially bad practices, which brings me to another fundamental hesitation I have about the bill.
We live in a democracy and the strength of the democracy itself depends on the thinking capacity of each individual citizen. As life becomes more complex, as the government intrudes more upon the ordinary lives of our citizens there is (1), a growing tendency for the government to interfere and (2), a growing tendency for the citizen to ask the government for more and more help. I suggest the best sort of citizen in this country is the one who believes in standing on his own feet, who most resents government interference and who seeks the least of the government. This is the man who realizes the heritage we have, who realizes the possibilities that exist in this country for a man of ability and courage.

It is that the 1951 amendment, now section 94A, was drawn purposely with the object in view of authorizing a simple contributory old age pension scheme on the basis of the report of the committee-I refer to the report of the all-party committee which met and which, as my hon. friend pointed out, was accepted by the government of that day-on the basis of their view that such a scheme should not be based on and should not include the wider benefits possible under any scheme resembling that of the

Old Age Security Act
United States. In other words, the 1951 amendment was drawn having in mind purely and simply a contributory old age pension scheme with benefits payable by virtue of old age and for no other reason. That is why any scheme which contemplates the extension of such benefits to disability and survivors benefits must have the authority of a constitutional amendment.
What we now want, on the basis of the explanation of our proposal given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), and repeated by my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) is authority to include such matters as disability and survivors benefits and possibly the regulation of private pension plans, including portability. All these are things which I point out to you are not necessarily embraced within the half-baked first scheme or even the amended scheme put forward by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson)- but they are in a category-that is to say disability and survivor benefits and the regulation of private pension plans including portability-which are not necessarily incidental to old age pensions. They are not necessarily incidental thereto and they are therefore in a category which might otherwise be struck down by the courts if the legislation establishing them is not covered by a constitutional amendment broad enough to include them without question.
As I have pointed out, this is established by the opinion of 1958 which is reproduced in the Clark report. That is why the letter sent by the Prime Minister to the provincial premiers includes the following statement:
The law officers of the crown advise me that this authority-
This authority being section 94A.
-would permit parliament to enact a contributory, graduated old age pension plan but would not permit the inclusion of benefits payable under certain circumstances to widows and children, nor to contributors who become disabled before they are old. To extend the law in this most desirable way, it would be necessary to replace the present section with one reading as follows:
Then the proposed amendment to section 94A is reproduced. I may say that I am reading there from the appendix to Hansard of January 22.
Indeed, I might point out that in our discussions with the provinces to date there has been an indication that the proposed amendment is not wide enough to accomplish the objective we have in mind. I refer specifically of course to the letter from the premier of Saskatchewan which was tabled in this house today and in which Mr. Lloyd suggests that the proposed section 94A-that is to say the amendment we propose-could be interpreted by the courts as being too narrow to

cover a contributory graduated old age pension plan which would include pensions to widows and children and to contributors who become disabled before they are old.
We do not accept that view. However, I mention it in order to point out that here is a provincial premier writing, with the advice of his constitutional advisers, to say that possibly the amendment we propose does not go far enough to enable it to embrace the things which we want to see in such a scheme. Although we do not accept that view, I suggest that it is as valid as is the view of my hon. friend, or indeed that it is more valid than is the view of my friend the hon. member for Essex East who says, on the basis of an authority which he does not cite, that we do not need any amendment at all to section 94A in order to include such a scheme.

We are seriously disappointed that the government has not presented an over-all retirement plan as a result of the opportunity it has had to study the well publicized Clark report, I want to say before I go any further, because I want to be as non-partisan and constructive as possible, as is the practice of the group for whom I am speaking at the moment, that we dislike the question of old age security and related legislation being placed on the auction block of election expediency from year to year.
