I am sure that all of us will agree that all members are aware of the need for an overall retirement pension plan covering all groups in our society. All members recognize the responsibility of this parliament to the people of Canada to provide this plan as soon as possible. I am sure all of us recognize that this nation has the financial ability to meet the needs and the rights of our senior citizens to participate in the benefits of production and the standard of living that the great majority enjoy at the present time.
I have read a lot on this subject and I am really going to be quite brief. But I do want to make my voice heard on this occasion because I have spent all my life fighting for the underdog or on occasions tilting at windmills.
I thought this was a very good paragraph in an article by Mr. Harry J. Waisglass in the Canadian Welfare magazine of July 15, 1961. When describing the right of our senior citizens to participate in the wealth of the nation, he had this to say:
Another objective of social security systems might be to distribute productivity gains more equitably, not only between economic classes or between geographical regions within the nation but also between the various generations of the population. The aged have a right to share in current productivity gains, which are attributable largely to the contributions of earlier generations in building our current stock of social and business capital and technology.
[Mr. Herridge.l
This measure is a recognition, to a limited extent, of the right of our senior citizens to gain from this increase in our national productivity. As I said before, I do not think anyone in this house questions the ability of the Canadian nation to finance a sound and equitable national pension scheme to cover all our citizens. I think the great difference of opinion is as to method and as to the mechanics of the scheme. That is where the great difference of opinion comes.
We believe, Mr. Speaker, as other speakers have mentioned before, that the plan should provide a basic security pension for our industrial workers, farmers, self-employed persons, those in the public service, in fact all Canadians. This is going to mean considerable integration of private and public pension plans in an over-all national pension scheme.
How should it be financed? We in this group believe it should be financed in two or three ways. First, it should be financed by a measure of taxation which has to be determined by the circumstances of the time. Second, it should be financed by contributions from the employer, from the employed and from the self-employed. Third, we stress that under present circumstances pension funds are largely invested by insurance companies in certain companies and private investment schemes across the country. We in this group believe there is an excellent way of financing this pension plan, while at the same time providing the funds that are necessary for certain national publicly owned projects in this country. This plan could be partly financed also from the profits on invested funds, contributions and so on, in public ownership projects, such as power projects, highways, hospitals, schools and necessary services. All of these are self-liquidating projects. We believe that if we mobilize public interest in this, mobilize shall I say that sense of participation in the national pension scheme and in the investment of these funds in self-liquidating projects like the Mica creek dam that has been proposed, a method of financing would be found. Whether you have a capitalist or a socialist society, you cannot operate successfully without having a surplus.

There are two reasons I wish to speak on this bill. One is that as a result of climatic conditions in Comox-Alberni, we have a higher percentage of old age pensioners than any other part of Canada. Another reason is that I happen to occupy a seat that was held by one of the greatest members who ever sat in this parliament, the late A. W. Neill. Despite all the protestations of the Liberal party and new party, the late A. W. Neill played a very important part in bringing about the introduction of old age pensions in Canada. He was an independent member for Comox-Alberni and, as such, his support was badly needed by the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King in 1926, in order to retain power as government.
Mr. Neill has often told me the story and I may be pardoned for going back into history a little bit because that has been done so many times today. This is an entirely different story from what I have heard from members of the new party group and of the Liberal party, and I believe most of us will find it interesting. In order to win Mr. Neill's support, the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King undertook- and he was working with the late Mr. Heaps and the late Mr. Woodsworth-to introduce old age pensions. Mr. Neill told me "We had everything set. The Prime Minister agreed to introduce the legislation. He did introduce the legislation but behind our backs he made a deal with members of the other house to kill the legislation when it reached there." In view of statements and press reports of

Old Age Security Act
speeches made by some of the leading lights in the Liberal party, I wonder whether this legislation is not also going to be killed in the other place. I leave that thought in your minds.
The new party group are loud in their protestations and appeals for greater help for the old age pensioners and for the middle-aged who cannot fit themselves into industry. I am going to suggest one way by which they and their colleagues, the labour unions, might help. It is a suggestion I want my hon. friend from Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) to listen to, because I think he will go along with the idea. There are few companies in Canada today which do not operate under a union agreement in which there is a maintenance of members or, in other words, a closed shop.
From experience I know there are often casual part time jobs which could be quite well filled by old age pensioners and others who have found themselves unemployed in their later working years. There is a still greater number of jobs that might be filled by those over 55 years of age but, in every case where there is a union agreement, the union insists that should these men be employed they must become members of the union and pay dues regularly. This is an unfair imposition on old age pensioners, and particularly on men past 50 years of age who find themselves unemployed. To join some unions costs $100 and the dues run as high as $9 or $10 per month.
Last fall I learned of a case where a union official insisted on a man 66 years of age joining the union at a cost of $100, or else leaving his job. At the same time, union officials were pressing an old age pensioner, another employee of that particular company, to join the union. However, I made it very plain that if they insisted I would make a public issue of it. In that case they did not insist, but many times they do get away with their bluff.
As I say, it is most unfair of the labour unions, the colleagues of the New Democratic party, to insist upon dues being paid by old age pensioners who are trying to eke out a living, and I believe the members of the new party should prevail on their union colleagues to cease this practice.
I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Essex East, who reminded me a good deal of the blue jays I see in my garden. Once in a while I chase them out of my berry patch and they fly up onto the limbs of a tree, chattering away. When I throw a stone at them they fly to another tree and keep on chattering. They never stop and, so far as I am concerned, I shall always think of the

hon. member for Essex East as a blue jay or camp robber. Sometimes those birds are known as whisky-jacks.

U.S. Social Security like a giant lottery-The United States old age pensions system-known as social security-is somewhat like a giant lottery where most contributors get something in return but a few persons get the big prizes.
In operation for a quarter century, the contributory system provides for monthly pensions ranging from $40 to $127 for single persons and from $60 to $191 for married couples.
Built up through a special tax levied on wage-earners, employers and the self-employed, this pension is payable to contributors reaching the age of 65. A reduced pension is paid to those retiring at 62.
A survey by the social security administration shows that 58 per cent of the beneficiaries are receiving $75 a month or less. About 41 per cent get $55 a month or less and 21 per cent get $40 or less.

improvements to old age pension legislation can successfully claim for itself total credit for the legislation or for the improvements that are being brought forward.
I had an opportunity to sit in this house from 1945 to 1957 while a Liberal administration was in office. The former minister of national health and welfare, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), will agree with me, I believe, when I say that over the years many distinguished members of the C.C.F. party have been helpful in parliament and throughout the country in building a climate which would make improvements in old age pensions possible and acceptable. I think that when we are debating the particular scheme before us at this time all parties in this house conscientiously believe that improvements should be made in our old age security legislation. There may be differences as to degree; there may be differences as to timing, but certainly we want something to be done.
The government in bringing in a measure to increase old age security pensions by $10 a month says it has another scheme, and requires a constitutional amendment in order to provide a national retirement plan. Both the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) say that the government's proposals in this regard are based on the Clark report. Then they say that one of the main reasons, if not the chief reason, why they are convinced they require a constitutional amendment is that the need for such an amendment has been pointed out in the Clark report. Well, the government has had the Clark report for three years. I have in my hand the first volume-the second was issued on the same date-and the letter signed by Robert M. Clark and addressed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare is dated February 12, 1959. What has been the situation in this house? Opposition members of both parties have asked the government from time to time when it intended to take action on the Clark report. What was the standard reply? The government said: we are studying it; we are giving consideration to it. For three long years needy old age pensioners have waited upon a government which has looked upon them in a somewhat callous manner during this period. This present measure is, of course, something of a deathbed repentance. It certainly is a repentance very close to election day. Now the government is saying: Trust us; we shall bring it in and we shall look after you if you return us for another period.
A few years ago the C.C.F. party put forward a pension plan. It was laughed at and ridiculed by people who said it was going to
Old Age Security Act
cost too much. The country cannot afford it, they said. There is less ridicule today. The Liberal party has brought forward a plan which goes beyond what is proposed in this legislation. It is a plan which will provide a minimum of $75 a month for single persons- the same amount as was in the plan put forward by this party some years ago. The people of this country want the government to do more and I think this legislation will obtain the support of the Canadian people.
The proposal before us today will cost a great deal of money; old age pension legislation is expensive. But I think that in addition to considering the cost we should consider the plight of many of our retired citizens. We have campaigned for years to improve old age pensions, to increase the size of the payments and to make them applicable to a larger number of Canadian citizens. We have been making some real progress, but I do not think we have gone far enough. Some people have said the political parties are putting old age pensioners on the auction block. I am personally acquainted with a great many people who have retired and who have little or nothing more to live on than their old age pensions. They are interested in the position being taken by the various parties. They are interested in finding out whether or not one party is more advanced than another in this particular field.
I live in the small hamlet of Kay ville in Saskatchewan and along the street where I live there are a number of people who are in receipt of old age pensions. There are a number of widows, a number of widowers and a number of couples. As a matter of fact, there are so many people receiving old age pensions on this street that it is commonly known as pension avenue. I know these people personally, and some of them are having a very difficult time indeed. I ask hon. members to reflect and ask themselves how a person with an income of only $55 a month can survive if that income is not supplemented by other means. I think we all recognize that in talking about retirement plans we need to raise our sights and increase the amount of the pension. The plans will be based, to some extent, on the income of the person who obtains the pension during some period prior to his becoming eligible for that pension. One of the main purposes is to get an increase in the amount of the pension to retired persons. Hon. members from this side of the house have been advocating a pension of $75 a month. I speak, now, not from a position where I can state this as the policy of this party; rather, I am voicing my own opinion which I hope will be given consideration. I am suggesting that we should take steps, and take them immediately, to

make certain that people who are retired in this country shall have an income of not less than $100 a month. I do not think that is a fabulous figure even though I see some hon. members opposite are sneering.

The government is taking steps to provide $65 a month and I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare clearly recognizes that this sum is not sufficient. That recognition is revealed in a speech he made in this house on February 5 as reported at page 531 of Hansard when he stated:
Under the federal unemployment assistance program through which this is achieved-
He was speaking about further increases. I continue:
-there is no ceiling on the amount which the federal government will share in meeting the individual needs of older persons. It is left to the provinces to determine the upper limit of the additional assistance. For example, if a province were to decide that the upper limit should be $85 or even higher in relation to the special needs of the individual pensioner, we would be prepared to pay 5C per cent of the cost involved, that is of the cost over $65. The federal government would then actually be paying over 88 per cent of the $85.
I point this out to indicate that the minister is sympathetic to the need of providing more than $65 a month, at least in particular circumstances, and to show that in addition to the provisions of the Old Age Security Act and old age assistance the minister says part of the legislative program to deal with the needs of retired people is the Unemployment Assistance Act.
I suggest that we as parliamentarians should bring together when considering a program

of this nature the provisions of the Unemployment Assistance Act, the Old Age Security Act and the Old Age Assistance Act and should say we are prepared to provide a minimum pension of $100 a month based on a means test.
That would not mean that everyone upon reaching age 70 would receive $100 any more than under present conditions everyone upon reaching age 65 receives the old age pension. Of approximately 500,000 people in Canada between ages 65 and 70, about 21 per cent or just under 100,000 receive old age assistance I see no reason why the percentage above age 70 requiring this type of assistance would be much higher than 21 per cent although it might be a little higher.
The proposal I advance would not mean the payment of this additional sum to the wealthy or those with high incomes. However, the adoption of this proposal would provide everyone over age 65 with a minimum income of $100 a month.
The present proposals introduced by the minister will cost the government an additional $113.4 million. I do not have the advantage of the minister's technical staff but from information I have gleaned from his department, I suggest the proposal I have put forward would cost between $110 and $115 million. If my proposal were adopted the government would no longer have to pay through unemployment insurance its share of payments, formerly above $55 and now above the proposed $65 a month. The whole sum would not be an additional cost to the federal treasury. I am certain the government could work out with the provinces a means by which they would come in. The federal government might have to be more generous and pay more than 50 per cent but in any event my proposition would cost the federal treasury less than the total sum to which I have referred.
The adoption of my proposal would have this effect. Canadians who have reached age 65 would be assured of this minimum monthly income even before the retirement plan comes into effect, no matter what the plan might be. The adoption of my proposal would not mean an additional expenditure in this area every year from now on because after the retirement fund was built up-whether it be the scheme put forward by the government, the official opposition or the New Democratic party-the minimum income for almost everyone would be in excess of $100 a month. This cost would steadily diminish and would decrease to almost zero when the retirement plan, whichever scheme might be adopted, is fully operating.
I am suggesting that for people who have reached retirement age in this nation the 26207-1-40
Old Age Security Act
federal government, in co-operation with the provincial governments, should undertake action to provide this basic minimum income. Someone says, "Oh, that is putting back the means test". Every retirement plan that is put forward has in it a means test. It states that the amount of money going into the plan or being paid into the plan by any person shall be related to his income and that the pension paid out under the plan shall be related to the income, so that if you have a high income you get a relatively high pension. That is certainly a means test.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that this kind of proposal would take some working out and would require the co-operation of the provinces, but I am suggesting that it is a laudable objective to see to it that Canadians who have reached retirement age shall have a minimum income of much more than $65 or $75 a month.
The concept of old age pensions introduced many years ago was that the nation should undertake a measure to prevent grave hardship or to prevent people from becoming a burden on their relatives. I suggest that our concept now should be changed and that we are undertaking these measures to make it possible for Canadian citizens who have reached retirement age to go on enjoying a fair share of the great production of this country. I think the pension plan we are talking about today is a break-through. It means that we are moving from subsistence pensions to pensions based on a Canadian standard of living. The years ahead will prove that a $100 pension I have been advocating tonight is not fantastic and is not far fetched but is within the competence of governments of this country to provide.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to hold up the passage of this bill this evening but there are one or two remarks I want to make before it passes. I believe that all of us are treating this subject with the seriousness it deserves. I think all of us have old age pensioners in our constituencies. We might not have fishermen or wheat farmers, but we certainly are concerned about old age pensioners. I could not help feeling that there has been a slightly unfortunate emphasis during this debate. Perhaps if I were an elderly person I would feel like a beggar with my hat in my hand wondering on which side of the street to stand.
However, if anything has been proven by this debate it is that all three parties have played a major role in bringing about old age pensions in this country. Perhaps the emphasis should not be upon what we have done or, what we would have done, but rather it should be upon what we have invested in by this scheme. I feel we should take the emphasis off charity in so far as the old age pensioners are concerned. Surely what has happened over the past few years has convinced us whether we are farmers

or fishermen or storekeepers or lawyers that what we are really doing is investing in the elderly people. It is only through these transfer payments that we can keep our society going. This certainly has been proven by the events of this last winter when we had so many people unemployed because without the transfer payments by old age pensions, unemployment insurance, family allowances and so on, our whole economy might have broken down.
Surely, we should think about this and recognize that old age pensioners have no reason to thank us, no matter to what party we belong. We are lacking in markets. We are worried about foreign markets. Sometimes we forget that the most valuable market we have is the home market. The nearly one million old age pensioners which we have represent one of the most valuable markets we have, no matter in what part of the economy we happen to be working. I was very interested in listening to Dr. T. R. Langley, the retired chairman of Canadian General Electric. He was talking about this very matter, the fact that we cannot entirely depend upon increasing exports and production. We must look to our aged, to those people who are in the lower bracket of our economic system, to provide these markets for products which we are going to be producing in our industry.
My second and last point is that it is very unfortunate we have made political pawns of the aged. I think this strikes at the very basis of our whole political morality. I was talking to a doctor in my constituency last week end. He was saying to me, laughingly that it was too bad we did not have the old days in politics when you got a bottle of whiskey because then you knew what you were getting.

Prime Minister of Canada,

My dear Prime Minister,
I have submitted to my colleagues your letter of January 17, in which you suggest that the constitution be amended to enable the parliament of Canada to make laws in relation to
(b)	"pensions and other benefits incidental to, or conducive to the better operation and administration of, a scheme of old age pensions".
You will readily appreciate that we cannot come to a decision until accurate details of the pension scheme you intend to introduce are made available to us. We certainly could not submit to the legislative assembly a proposition such as the one you are now making without being able to explain clearly and fully what the proposed legislation is about.
You will no doubt recall that, before suggesting to the provinces the constitutional amendment made in 1951 with the consent of parliament and of all the legislatures, a joint committee of the Senate and the

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
House of Commons, of which I was joint chairman, had made a comprehensive study of the matter at public hearings. On the basis of the committee's report, the federal government was then in a position to make clearcut proposals to the provinces. When they accepted the suggested constitutional amendment the provinces, knew exactly what measure the government was going to submit to parliament.
I sincerely believe it to be essential that your government supply the provinces with the details of your plan before asking them to propose to their legislatures that they agree to a constitutional amendment.
Only when all the required information is available to us will it be possible for the Quebec government to have some opinion on the desirability of the proposed amendment.
I intend to table copies of your letter and of my reply in the Legislative Assembly next Tuesday.
Yours sincerely, (signed) Jean Lesage

Regina, February 2nd, 1962. The Right Honourable J. G. Diefenbaker, Q.C., Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Ontario.
My dear Prime Minister:
I am pleased to advise you that my colleagues and I concur with the federal government's proposed amendment to section 94A of the British North America Act as outlined in your letter of January 17, 1962. I assure you that the government of Saskatchewan will support any genuine effort on the part of the federal government to improve the Canadian social security system.
While we concur with the proposed amendment, I feel obliged to point out that our legal advisers have expressed some doubts about its wording. Their concern is that the proposed section 94A could be interpreted by the courts as being too narrow to cover a contributory graduated old age pension plan which would include pensions to widows and children and to contributors who become disabled before they are old.
If the government of Canada wishes to discuss in more detail Saskatchewan's reservations about the wording of the proposed amendment, we are prepared to do so at any time.
Yours sincerely,
W. S. Lloyd.

Ottawa, February 3, 1962. The Honourable Jean Lesage, P.C., M.P.P.,
Premier of Quebec,
Parliament Buildings,
Quebec City, Quebec.
My dear Premier:
I have considered the request in your letter of January 24 for more precise details of the pension plan we would ask parliament to establish under the extended powers we are proposing should be granted to parliament in section 94A of the British North America Act. You say you would not place before the legislature a proposal to amend the constitution without explicit details of the proposed legislation to be enacted by parliament after the constitutional amendment is made.
You and the premiers of the other provinces have already been informed of the essential feature that we wish to include in such legislation which requires an amendment to the British North America Act. The amendment is not one that diminishes in any way the powers of the provincial legislatures, for it would provide that no law passed under it would affect the operation of any provincial law relating to the same subjects.

Under the amendment we are proposing, parliament would be granted a slightly more extensive jurisdiction, to deal with old age pensions in a way that will also take account of the needs of widows and children and disabled persons. We are not proposing here the exercise of delegated legislative power or a joint dominion-provincial plan.
It is a recognized constitutional principle that a provincial legislature does not take responsibility for the explicit details of the terms in which parliament would use the powers given it by an amendment. Indeed the whole purpose of the amendment is to enable parliament to take that responsibility itself.
In the circumstances, therefore, I feel it would be improper for the government of Canada to submit for the approval of a provincial government and legislature the details of legislation which it is contemplated parliament would enact following such amendment.
I hope that you will give further consideration to the request contained in my letter of January 17, as many persons in all parts of Canada are asking for the benefits of the legislation which would follow this constitutional change and which, as I see it, would in no way affect the rights of provinces.
Yours sincerely,
John G. Diefenbaker
